4. Liquid retention and mechanical test ownership.

In a declared four-bridge geometry, each wetted radius is bounded by50um, surface tension by.6N/m and pressure difference by30kPa. The assumed resultant capillary/pressure force bound is
F<=n*(2*pi*r*gamma+pi*r^2*dp)=1.69646mN.
This requires the stated wetted geometry and pressure bounds; pinned films, larger wetting footprints or another meniscus can change it. It is not a measured pull-off force.

For100um-long ideal cylindrical bridges, introduced bulk resistivity1e-6ohm*m gives.0127324ohm per bridge. Four bridges occupy3.14159nL; introduced density8000kg/m3 gives25.1327micrograms. Interface films, contact constrictions and alloy chemistry are absent. These counts do not prove a working.1ohm connection, economical consumables, reversible wetting or cleaned receiving pads.

A.6x.3mm suction area at an introduced50kPa gives ideal9mN, larger than that modelled liquid force. But four probes at the P1 proposed.05N/tip load apply.2N,22.22 times that suction capacity. Successful transport does not supply the retained-open test fixture. A common capture cage, independent reaction path, substantially lighter probes or another observation organisation must be built. Probe pressure cannot silently close the gap or temporarily improve a contact whose service state is meant to be tested.

The state distinction is concrete: isolated component measurements should occur with every relevant physical conductor open while an actual holder retains the part. Final assembled resistance, leakage, bandwidth and physical function are then measured after the service load and probes withdraw. Neither test can replace the other, and no unbounded latent-defect detector follows.
